infotext.title: About these maps
infotext.text: The information presented in these maps is based on modeled predictions of fishing activity using vessel telemetry data (vessel monitoring system, VMS) that has been linked to landings data associated with each trip (Feist et al. 2021). The maps were generated in order to assess trends in fishing activity and how they might relate to large whale entanglements off the west coast of the United States from 2009 through mid-2016. Vessel speed and depth filters were used to identify where fishing activity was occurring, which is considered an approximation of where fishing may or may not be occurring. Further, not all vessels that fish for Dungeness crab are equipped with VMS transponders, with the proportion monitored being ~10%, ~50% and ~30% for Washington, Oregon and California, respectively. Fishing activity maps based on vessel telemetry should be used with caution, given the limitations and biases associated with the modeling methodology. Finally, the fishing activity mapping on these pages are based on the best available science at the time of their posting, but will be updated in the future as methods and source data, e.g., logbooks available in the states of Oregon and Washington, to better characterize fishing activity evolve and become available

infotext.title: Crab Fisheies Research
infotext.text:
On the U.S. West Coast, reports of whales entangled in fishing gear increased dramatically in 2014. In this study, a time-series of fishing activity maps were developed from 2009-2016 for the four fixed-gear fisheries most commonly implicated in entanglements. Maps were generated using vessel monitoring system (VMS) data linked to port-level landings databases, which were related to entangled whale reports over the same time period and with modelled distributions of humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae). Over the full study period, neither marked increases in fishing activity nor changes in fisheries footprints within regions with high whale densities were detected. In contrast, a delayed fishery opening in California due to a harmful algal bloom in spring of 2016 led to ~5–7 times average levels of Dungeness crab (Metacarcinus magister) fishing activity, which was consistent with a high rate of entanglement in that year. These results are consistent with current hypotheses that habitat compression caused by a marine heat wave increased the overlap of whales with fishing activity, despite minimal changes in the fisheries themselves. This study adds to literature on bycatch of protected species in otherwise sustainable fisheries, highlighting the value of using VMS data for reducing human-wildlife conflict in the ocean.

Geospatial data layers of Dungeness crab fishing activity off the U.S. West Coast at a 5km grid resolution using landings informed VMS data for posting to the CCIEA website. Data are binned in 4-month or annual intervals from the 2010-11 Dungeness crab season through June of 2016. Grid cells with fewer than 3 boats represented for any given time interval receive a value of 0. The data are considered non-confidential. Suggested value ranges for 4-month interval VMS ping count classes: <21; 21-35; 36-70; 71-140; 141-280; 281-560; >560. Suggested value ranges for annual interval VMS ping count classes: <50; 50-100; 101-200; 201-400; 401-800; 801-1600; >1600. See: Feist, BE, JF Samhouri, KA Forney & LE Saez (2021) Footprints of fixed gear fisheries in relation to rising whale entanglements on the U.S. West Coast. Fisheries Management & Ecology 28(3): 283-294. DOI: 10.1111/fme.12478
